cards.title: Missing discussion
cards.author: Naseer Memon
cards.why: It gathers the latest poverty, hunger and human development figures that are useful for Pakistan Affairs, Economy and essay papers.
cards.summary: The writer says official claims of economic stability hide a deep poverty and human development crisis. World Bank, UNDP, Global Hunger Index and mental health data all show conditions getting worse since 2018-19. He blames poor policy and governance, the decline of agriculture, high energy costs and insecurity that has driven away investors. He also criticises the media for ignoring these issues in favour of debates on governor's rule and new provinces.
key_facts: The World Bank's Pakistan Poverty and Equity brief says the national poverty rate rose from 22pc in 2018-19 to 29pc in 2024-25, about 70 million people.
Pakistan's Gini index rose from 28.4 to 32.7, the highest level of inequality in 25 years.
The UNDP's 2025 Global Multidimensional Poverty Index found 38.3pc of Pakistanis (95 million) multidimensionally poor, compared with 16.4pc in India and 14.9pc in Bangladesh.
The 2026 Global Hunger Index ranked Pakistan 106th of 122 countries, with the highest hunger score in South Asia.
The UNDP Human Development Report 2025 ranked Pakistan 168th of 193 countries, in the 'low' human development category.
A national mental health survey (2018-22) published in the British Medical Journal found that one in three Pakistanis has a diagnosable mental or behavioural disorder.

vocab.meaning: lack of basic needs such as health and education, not only lack of money
a child being too thin for his or her height because of poor nutrition
done only for show, without real effect

text: IN contrast to official claims of economic stability, a series of recently released reports provide disturbing evidence of deepening poverty and a human development crisis in Pakistan.

According to the World Bank’s Pakistan Poverty and Equity brief , the national poverty rate spiralled from 22 per cent in 2018-19 to 29pc in 2024-25 — meaning that about 70 million poor people across the country live below the national poverty line. The Gini index, a measure of economic inequality, has increased from 28.4pc to 32.7pc, the highest in 25 years. The World Bank’s regional economic outlook reported that Pakistan is home to about half of the MENAAP region’s population that falls under the extremely poor category. The World Bank attributes Pakistan’s reversal in poverty reduction to economic shocks triggered by the Covid-19 pandemic, the devastating 2022 floods, high inflation, and currency depreciation.

The UNDP’s 2025 Global Multidimensional Poverty Index reported that 38.3pc of Pakistan’s population (95m people) is multidimensionally poor — deprived not just of cash but also of necessities such as healthcare and education. Another 32m people are vulnerable to multidimensional poverty. Pakistan’s poor population of 38.3pc dwarfed India’s 16.4pc and Bangladesh’s 14.9pc.

The alarming scale of deprivation was also reflected in the 2026 Global Hunger Index, which placed Pakistan 106th among 122 countries. Pakistan has the highest hunger score in South Asia. The report attributes food price inflation to declining household purchasing power and constrained access to food. It finds that undernourishment in the country climbed from ‘low’ in 2018 to ‘medium’, while child wasting has risen towards the ‘high’ threshold.
Poverty is rooted in decades of misguided public policy.

All these reports reflect the severity of the crisis. A nationally representative mental health survey (2018-22), published in the British Medical Journal, revealed distressing facts. The survey found that every third Pakistani lives with a diagnosable mental or behavioural disorder; one in five meets the criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder. A shocking 6pc reported suicidal thoughts, and more than one in 10 had depression. Such staggering rates of mental disorders have been linked to lower income and poor education, unemployment, age, and disrupted family circumstances.

Human development has remained a chronically ignored priority in Pakistan. The UNDP’s Human Development Report 2025 placed Pakistan 168th out of 193 countries appearing in the ‘low’ human development category. Except for Afghanistan, all regional countries ranked ahead of Pakistan on the Human Development Index.

Poverty is rooted in decades of misguided public policy and bad governance. Human development has been given cosmetic importance — the subject is mostly confined to official speeches and election manifestos. Although Covid-19, the floods, and broader climate change have battered the economy, human development seldom features on the government’s list of priorities.

Geopolitical and ongoing border tensions, and more recently the Gulf war shocks, have diverted resources and attention from human development to security priorities. The issue has been further compounded by internal security challenges that have held back exports and stifled foreign investment. Terrorism in two provinces and the poor law and order situation have shattered local investments. This environment has forced many foreign companies to pack up and withdraw capital from our markets.

Agriculture — for long the bedrock of the national economy and a source of food security for millions — has been systematically eroded in recent decades. Sha­rp increases in agri-input prices, a poorly managed water sector, rapid land degradation, and exploitative market forces have wrecked this critical sector. Soaring energy prices, an unreliable grid, and a huge tax burden, including petroleum surcharges, have made energy exorbitant for the farm sector. Crippling increases in petroleum prices have pushed up transport fares, raising the cost of the farm-to-market supply chain. The resulting food inflation has forced millions of families to compromise on their diet.

Sadly, even though poverty and hunger have emerged as an existential challenge for millions of families in Pakistan, a national focus on these issues is absent. These issues rarely find space in the national discourse — especially on electronic media, which remains abuzz with hysterical talk shows on subjects like governor’s rule and new provinces. Distracting the masses from the real issues and failing to include critical report findings will not reduce the citizens’ frustration.
The writer is senior adviser, water governance, at the Sustainable Development Policy Institute.
naseer_memon@sdpi.org
Published in Dawn, November 10th, 2026

cards.title: Economic ills
cards.author: Dr Niaz Murtaza
cards.why: It offers comparative economic indicators useful for questions on Pakistan's structural economic problems.
cards.summary: The writer argues that Pakistan's economic stabilisation is oversold and that key indicators remain weak. Per capita growth has been close to zero since 2024, investment is low, exports are small and tax revenue is among the lowest in South Asia. He says the country depends on remittances, borrowing and deposits from rich states, while interest payments leave little for development. He blames a 'parasitic' ruling elite and argues that only democracy and civilian control can bring reform.
key_facts: Pakistan's GDP is about 82pc consumption and only 14pc investment, while India and China invest over 30pc of GDP.
Pakistan's exports fell from a peak of 17pc of GDP in 1992 to about a tenth of GDP now.
Harvard's Economic Complexity Index ranks Pakistan 89th among 145 countries.
Pakistan's tax revenue is about 11pc of GDP, among the lowest in South Asia.
Pakistan's public debt-to-GDP ratio is 73pc.
Industry's share of Pakistan's economy has stayed at about a fifth for over 50 years, against a third in Bangladesh.

vocab.meaning: a ruler who uses power to steal public wealth
a heavy burden, such as debt, that holds back progress
very unpleasant or unfair

text: DESPITE an oversold stabilisation, many of our economy’s vital signs continue to falter. The economy resembles a patient out of the ICU but still in hospital.

Since 2024, our per capita GDP growth has been near zero — sadly, South Asia’s slowest recorded pace. Even our recent growth spurts, brief and import-led, have given way to longer busts, draining reserves and sending us back to the IMF’s tough terms that extend low growth.

Once near the region’s top performers in per capita GDP, we now risk falling to the bottom. As incomes stall, poverty rises. Our extreme poverty rate (23 per cent) is near the bottom regionally . It’s about 10 times India’s, against near parity in 2011.

Our GDP’s composition tells a bleak tale too. It’s consumption-heavy (82pc) but investment-light (14pc) — on both counts among the region’s worst. India and China invest over 30pc of GDP, creating jobs and capacity for today and later — much better than our consumption binges. Limiting job, technology, and export growth, industry’s share has been nearly a fifth for over 50 years versus a quarter in India and Sri Lanka and a third in Bangladesh.

Low investment causes low growth, but its origins and destinations matter too. We court foreign capital while ignoring local capital. Foreign capital must earn and save more dollars than it repatriates and create jobs and local capacity. But we get it mostly in domestic sectors, which later depletes reserves.

Unlike our peers, we chase a few rich states for capital rather than prioritising diversified private capital. We shun creative ways to boost local savings and capital. So, we remain capital-starved — yet we quickly drain reserves and risk the haughty whims of rich states.

Capital droughts in export sectors cause dollar and job droughts. From a peak of 17pc in 1992, exports now barely reach a tenth of our GDP — South Asia’s second-lowest share, below even Afghanistan’s. Low-quality compounds low quantity. Harvard’s Economic Complexity Index ranks us 89th among 145 states. So our exports face intense competition but return little. Exports rarely cover imports, creating large trade gaps.
Dreary metrics mirror a sinking economy.
Remittances partly plug the gap. But exports keep workers at home and families intact, create jobs, earn dollars, and pay taxes.

Remittances separate families and often don’t create jobs or pay taxes directly. They frequently fuel consumption, while exports are fuelled by investment. Remittances now almost equal our exports, as it is easier to send workers abroad than goods (India earns six times as much from exports as from remittances). Even so, we often run large external deficits that lead to a crisis as booms turn into busts.

Low growth and weak efforts leave our coffers lean. Tax revenues barely reach 11pc of GDP — which is among South Asia’s lowest. Indirect anti-poor taxes provide about half our tax target, down from about two-thirds in 2021-22. New direct taxes further burden the wallets of salaried persons and formal industry, while favoured sectors pay low taxes. Spending prioritises upkeep over uplift. Expenditure hogs over 90 paisas out of every federal budget rupee; development consoles itself with just five.

These twin deficits force us to keep our borrowing bowl out. Our public debt-to-GDP ratio of 73pc is lower than the Japanese and Singaporean levels of over 150pc. But our repayment muscle better depicts our debt overhang.

On the share of federal outlays spent on interest alone, we rank among the worst globally. We use debt not only to invest or meet recurrent expenses but also to beef up rese­rves. IMF debt and deposits by rich states, which impose odious economic and political conditions on us, now exceed even our highest-ever reserves. These dre­ary metrics mirror a sinking economy. Low investment and import-led growth widen the twin deficits to swell debt. Interest outlays then leave little money for growth, creating a vicious circle.

A weak economy reflects perverse politics. Poor countries need both a developmental and a welfare state. Ours is a parasitic and apathetic state run by rapacious rulers. This isn’t a tragedy of ineptitude alone: willing rulers can easily hire merit. It’s a deliberate design by kleptocrats who may lose their wealth and power if there is real progress.

Nor is this the tale of a few eras. Our autocracies, too, delivered short-term growth, leading to conflict and undercutting future progress. Ideas abound on how to pursue sound progress, but minds that will champion and implement them well do not. Only democracy and civilian sway will bring such minds to the helm of affairs.
The writer has a PhD degree in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 30 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.

cards.title: Restructuring plans
cards.author: Editorial
cards.why: New provinces, constitutional amendments and local government are recurring Pakistan Affairs and Governance topics.
cards.summary: The editorial notes that talk of new provinces is growing, even though the PPP, a coalition partner, opposes it. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistan could have up to 12 new provinces if the work were based on administrative needs. There is speculation that a 28th constitutional amendment may be passed quickly, with implementation after the next election. The paper says such a change needs consensus and should wait until after a trusted election, and that empowered local governments could meet the same needs.
key_facts: Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistan could have as many as 12 new provinces if they were drawn on administrative grounds.
Administrative restructuring is reportedly being considered through a 28th amendment to the Constitution.
The PPP, a key coalition partner, opposes the creation of new provinces.
The editorial argues that local governments were meant to be the last-mile tier of service delivery but have not been made effective.

vocab.meaning: the period of time between two events
the ability to produce the intended result

text: NO matter how strongly the PPP, a key coalition partner, wishes to see it buried , the push for new administrative units and provinces seems to be picking up steam once again.

Defence Minister Khawaja Asif brought the issue into the limelight on Sunday, telling an interviewer that the country could have as many as 12 new provinces if the exercise were driven by administrative needs rather than ethnic, linguistic, or political considerations. Yet in Pakistan, redrawn boundaries always carry ethnic and political weight.

Speculation about a possible administrative restructuring has intensified of late, with talk of it soon being accomplished through a 28th amendment to the Constitution. It is also suggested that while the amendment may be fast-tracked, perhaps wrapped up within the year, its actual implementation will be deferred until after the next general election because of the formidable legal and administrative challenges involved in redistributing the state’s resources equitably.
But if the implementation can wait, why not the legislation?

The government may be tempted to push ahead while it can still count on a majority in parliament, but a majority alone is not a consensus. A proposal of such immense national import demands nothing less.

The Election Commission’s botched conduct of the 2024 general election has also left serious, lingering doubts about how far the current legislature represents the public will — doubts that might taint any constitutional change of this magnitude that it passes. It would, therefore, be a much wiser move, politically speaking, to take up any debate on administrative restructuring again after the next general election.

In the interim, parliament should pursue electoral reforms with the opposition to ensure that the commission does not repeat its 2024 mistakes, so that the next election earns the public’s trust and yields a legislature whose mandate is beyond doubt.

Until then, the federal and provincial governments should at least make an effort to revive the local government structure and give it a fair chance to prove its efficacy as a means of public service delivery.

Most arguments in favour of new administrative units circle back to a few central ideas, chief among which is the failure of provincial governments to ensure that resources allocated to them reach the people. The LG system was designed to be that last-mile tier of governance that would make this possible, but, sadly, successive civilian governments have failed to operationalise it effectively, preferring instead to concentrate administrative, political and financial power in a few provincial centres.

Population growth and internal migration have sharply increased pressures on existing administrative centres in recent decades, but empowered LGs can redistribute that burden without redrawing provincial boundaries.
It is up to the political leadership to choose between these two paths.
Published in Dawn, November 10th, 2026

cards.title: Served by the court
cards.author: Arifa Noor
cards.why: It explains how the new constitutional court is shaping fundamental rights, electoral disputes and women's rights.
cards.summary: The writer reviews three judgements of the new Federal Constitutional Court (FCC). It dismissed the JUI-F's appeal over a reserved seat given to Sadaf Ihsan, whom the party says was never on its list. It also stopped the Peshawar High Court from hearing cases on PTI workers' arrests and bail, saying Article 199 powers could not be used once the army was called in aid of civil power. In a third case, it limited workplace harassment to conduct of a sexual nature, unlike earlier, broader rulings.
key_facts: The Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the JUI-F's appeal against the ECP decision reinstating Sadaf Ihsan in a reserved seat.
More than 60 bail orders were challenged by the KP government in the FCC.
The FCC barred the Peshawar High Court from hearing these matters under Article 199 because the army had been called in aid of civil power in KP.
The FCC ruled that workplace harassment is limited to overtly sexual conduct, departing from earlier judgements that included gender-based discrimination.
Amendments to the harassment law itself now give a wider definition of harassment.

vocab.meaning: a temporary relief from a decision or punishment
to pretend to be another person
a request to a high court to protect legal or fundamental rights

text: LAST week, the newly established Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) gave two noteworthy judgements. Both concerned legal issues of a political nature — the kind that perhaps would have taken up considerable time and energy in the Supreme Court of the olden days, along with detailed coverage by the media. But those were different times; at present, the cases progressed quietly and the decisions came without much bang or thunder.

In one case, the court settled an election dispute that has been going on for the past two years. Back in 2024, the JUI-F had disputed the notification of a woman to one of its reserved seats. It claimed that the woman who had been notified simply shared the first name — Sadaf — with the woman mentioned on the party’s list. The woman on the JUI-F list, Sadaf Yasmin, had decided against submitting her papers due to personal reasons; however, a woman called Sadaf Ihsan (with whom the party says it has no connection) submitted her papers and got nominated by the ECP for the seat. The JUI-F claims Ihsan impersonated Sadaf Yasmin despite having a different name and was somehow identified as the latter.

When this was pointed out to the Election Commission of Pakistan , not only did it withdraw the announcement, but also suspended the official who issued the notification. This was reported in Dawn . But the matter didn’t end there. Sadaf Ihsan approached the Peshawar High Court (PHC) and was reinstated. The party then challenged the decision in the Supreme Court, winning reprieve for itself. Ihsan was suspended. But the relief was simply an interim order, and once the FCC was established, the file was transferred to it.

The FCC sent the case back to the ECP, which in January this year reinstated Sadaf Ihsan in the seat. This past week, the JUI-F’s appeal against this decision was dismissed by the FCC. Ihsan is now a JUI-F MNA, while the party continues to insist that she is not a member and was never on the list submitted to the ECP. Ihsan, according to a report on the Fafen website, claims she and her family are associated with the party.
Three cases, three judgements. But they reveal quite a lot of what the court appears to stand for.

It now appears the decision is final and no appellate forums remain. Another interesting aspect of this case is that this seat was given to the JUI-F after the decision that deprived the PTI of reserved seats.

In a second case, the FCC has apparently stopped the PHC from hearing cases regarding the custody or arrest of PTI workers. With the imposition of the emergency in KP and a crackdown against the party in the province, multiple cases concerning the whereabouts or bail of PTI members ended up in the PHC, which then passed an interim order preventing such detentions.

As in many cases, bail had also been granted; the provincial government challenged them in the FCC. According to one report in Dawn , more than 60 cases in which bail had been given were challenged by the KP government in the FCC. After hearing the cases, the FCC stopped the high court from hearing these matters; its argument was that since the army has been called in, in aid of civil power, the court could no longer hear matters under Article 199, which, in layperson’s terms, is equivalent to what we once saw as the suo motu powers of the Supreme Court.

According to one lawyer’s comment, which he posted on social media, this order means the high court can no longer entertain any writ petitions, which, according to him, is a power the courts continued to enjoy even under martial law regimes. In other words, the order limits the PHC in matters far wider than simply the arrests of and bail for PTI workers. It means the high court cannot hear any matters related to fundamental rights.

While these two cases date back to just the past week, a third judgement is a little older. It had already been discussed in quite a bit of detail in Dawn and elsewhere. But it is still worth mentioning.

In a recent case, the FCC seems to have provided a restricted interpretation of workplace harassment. Ignoring past precedents, which had interpreted workplace harassment more liberally, the court has now ruled that harassment is to be limited to actions of an overtly sexual nature; previously, judgements had interpreted the law to include what is defined as gender-based discrimination.

A piece by Barrister Rida Hosain pointed out that in a previous decision, Justice Ayesha Malik had said that “reducing harassment to conduct that is sexual in nature ‘takes away the essence’ of the harassment law, and ignores that harassment is often less about sexual interest and more about reinforcing existing power dynamics”. Hosain quoted Justice Ayesha Malik as saying that the very “purpose of harassment laws is to address gender-based discrimination at the workplace and not to limit it to sexual forms of harassment”. But the FCC has now seen it differently.

And while the decision drew criticism, it is fortunate that amendments to the law itself have provided a more wide-ranging definition. However, the ruling of the FCC does mean that complainants in incidents or cases that predate the amendment may have to prove harassment according to the FCC’s interpretation. Women lawyers in particular have discussed this issue in detail in articles and commentary that have appeared in Dawn .

Three cases, three judgements. But they reveal quite a lot of what the FCC appears to stand for — to those of us who have little understanding of the legalese but who do keep an eye on the politics of the country — be it fundamental rights, women’s rights, or perhaps those of political parties. One can only wonder if any of the parliamentarians who voted for these courts have paid any attention to these judgements.
The writer is a journalist.
Published in Dawn, November 10th, 2026

cards.title: Extreme heat
cards.author: Editorial
cards.why: It links climate change with food security and rural poverty, a common essay and Environment theme.
cards.summary: The editorial discusses a new UN assessment, 'Extreme Heat and Agriculture', by the FAO and the World Meteorological Organisation. It shows rising temperatures are cutting farm output, especially in rain-fed areas, and hurting rural incomes and diets. Punjab is badly affected, with fruit output halved in high-rainfall areas and heat stress lowering milk yields. The paper calls for heat-resistant crops, better water management, cold storage and cooperation with India on farm resilience.
key_facts: The FAO and World Meteorological Organisation published an assessment titled 'Extreme Heat and Agriculture'.
Fruit productivity in Punjab's high-rainfall areas has halved due to heat.
Heat stress is reducing milk production and increasing disease among small ruminants.
Pregnant and lactating rural women face a sharp rise in the risk of premature births during severe heatwaves.
Agriculture sustains about two-thirds of Pakistan's population.

vocab.meaning: an animal like a goat or sheep that chews its food again
food that goes bad quickly
producing breast milk

text: CLIMATE change is already taking its toll on Pakistan’s farm sector. Crop yields are falling, livestock productivity is declining, fertile land is becoming uncultivable, and food insecurity is rising. Alongside, rural incomes are shrinking, and both cash and food poverty are increasing.

It is against this backdrop that a new UN assessment — Extreme Heat and Agriculture — by the Food and Agriculture Organisation and the World Meteorological Organisation has sought to underscore the rapid erosion of farm productivity, especially in rain-fed regions, and its impact on rural households owing to rising temperatures across the country. The findings are particularly worrying for Punjab, where frequent and severe heatwaves are disrupting rural livelihoods. Fruit productivity in the province’s high-rainfall areas has halved. Livestock is suffering, with heat stress reducing milk production and increasing the incidence of diseases among small ruminants.

The consequences are not confined to farms. Lower output means reduced incomes for farming households, with extreme temperatures accelerating the spoilage of vegetables, dairy products, and other perishables. Families earn and eat less. Gender inequality deepens the problem. Rural women , who undertake considerable agricultural and household work, face prolonged exposure to extreme temperatures. Pregnant and lactating women are particularly vulnerable, with a sharp increase in the risk of premature births during severe heatwaves.

However, climate adaptation is yet to find a place in our agricultural policies. The effects of rising temperatures on the sector that sustains two-thirds of the population cannot be mitigated with input subsidies, crop support prices, or procurement targets. Farmers need heat-resistant crop varieties, better water management technology , and access to modern farming machinery. Investment in cold storage, efficient supply chains and public and livestock health services is equally important. Agricultural research requires greater private investment and better human resources.

Without tweaking policies to respond to the climate challenge, repeated heatwaves will erode productivity, making farming less viable for smallholders. The problem crosses the border. Both sides of Punjab face the same climate challenges, requiring Pakistan and India to cooperate on farm resilience. Heat is already cutting into rural incomes and into what families can afford to eat. Farm policies that ignore it will fail the people they are meant to support.
Published in Dawn, November 10th, 2026

cards.author: Jawed Naqvi
cards.why: It gives context on the US midterms and on the evolution of South Asian progressive politics.
cards.summary: The writer welcomes progressive wins in the US midterm elections, such as Abdul El-Sayed's Senate victory, but warns of a conservative pushback inside the Democratic Party. cards.title: Climate justice for Pakistan
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: Climate finance and Pakistan's vulnerability are core Environment and Foreign Policy topics.
cards.summary: The editorial says COP31 in Antalya has opened with a fight over climate money, and that for Pakistan this is a matter of survival. Pakistan emits less than 1pc of global emissions but is among the 10 most climate-vulnerable countries. It needs huge sums for its climate goals, yet debt servicing takes most revenue and the Loss and Damage Fund is very small. The paper suggests a 'mountain coalition' with Nepal, Bhutan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan and more lobbying for grant-based finance.
key_facts: Pakistan contributes less than 1pc of global greenhouse gas emissions but ranks among the 10 most climate-vulnerable countries.
The 2022 floods submerged a third of Pakistan, affected 33 million people and caused over $30 billion in damage.
Pakistan estimates it needs $565 billion by 2035 to meet its climate commitments.
The Loss and Damage Fund has $342 million available against $2.8 billion in requests.
Pakistan's $58 million in Loss and Damage Fund proposals received no allocation.
More than 60pc of Pakistan's revenues go to debt servicing.

vocab.meaning: causing loss of hope

text: COP31 has opened in Antalya with the same familiar and dispiriting contest over money. The UN Secretary-General has urged leaders to "get serious" about a crisis that is no longer a forecast but a daily emergency. Yet, developing nations have had to fight just to put climate finance on the official agenda. For countries like Pakistan, this is not just a diplomatic spectacle. It is a matter of survival. Pakistan has a negligible carbon footprint - it contributes less than 1% of global emissions - but ranks among the 10 most climate-vulnerable countries, exposed to heatwaves, extreme monsoons and accelerating glacial melt. The 2022 super-floods submerged a third of the country, affected 33 million people and caused over $30 billion in damage. Islamabad now estimates that meeting its climate commitments will require $565 billion by 2035. Where that money will come from is anyone's guess, though self-financing is not a real option - more than 60% of revenues are currently consumed by debt servicing alone. Pakistan's negotiating priorities are clear - accessible adaptation finance, predictable grant-based loss-and-damage support, and international recognition of threats, including mountain climate risks. As things stand, the Loss and Damage Fund is still embarrassingly small - $342 million available against $2.8 billion in requests, with Pakistan's own $58 million in proposals receiving no allocation. Experts have suggested that Pakistan build a 'mountain coalition' with countries such as Nepal, Bhutan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan to demand glacier monitoring, early-warning systems and resilient infrastructure. Islamabad should also use ties with China and G77 countries to lobby for more grant-based finance options that will not push affected countries further into debt. And though we can't give much in return, we can at least offer to try improving domestic transparency for donors' funds - though that may be an even more difficult task.

cards.title: The uniting opposition
cards.author: editorial
cards.why: It explains current opposition politics and the issues of governor's rule and new provinces.

The JUI-F, led by Maulana Fazlur Rehman, is reportedly in talks with TTAP.
Governor's rule has been imposed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

cards.title: Centre spent Rs5tr on devolved subjects in violation of Constitution, Senate panel head says
cards.author: Iftikhar A. Khan
cards.why: It concerns the 18th Amendment, federal-provincial relations and provincial quotas in federal service.
cards.summary: A Senate sub-committee head, Senator Zamir Hussain Ghumro, said the federal government spent over Rs5 trillion on devolved provincial subjects and CCI matters in violation of the Constitution, citing the Auditor General's report. He said the CCI and Cabinet Division had asked the prime minister to abolish 24 ministries and institutions. The panel also pressed for filling shortfalls in Balochistan's and Sindh's shares of federal jobs under Article 38(g). Separately, another Senate panel was briefed on the FIA probe into a silver swapping case.
key_facts: Senator Zamir Hussain Ghumro said the federal government spent over Rs5 trillion (over $18 billion) on devolved subjects and CCI matters.
Article 154 of the Constitution deals with the functions and rules of procedure of the Council of Common Interests.
The CCI and Cabinet Division sent summaries to the prime minister to abolish 24 ministries and institutions.
Article 38(g) of the Constitution provides for provincial shares in federal service; the panel found a shortage of over 30,000 jobs in Balochistan's share and over 80,000 in Sindh's.
The Establishment Division advertised 5,000 jobs for Balochistan to correct its share.
In the silver swapping case, about 400kg of silver was swapped with lead bars and 214kg has been recovered.

vocab.meaning: transferred from the central government to the provinces
a particular method of doing something

text: ISLAMABAD: The federal government spent more than Rs5 trillion on devolved provincial subjects and on ministries created on Council of Common Interests (CCI) matters in violation of the Constitution, the head of a Senate panel claimed on Tuesday.

Citing data from the report of the Auditor General of Pakistan, Senator Barrister Zamir Hussain Ghumro, chairing a sub-committee of the Senate Functional Committee on Devolution, said the figure was equivalent to more than $18 billion.
The convener said the country was facing twin issues of exorbitant federal expenditure and heavy borrowing totalling $135bn.

“At present, federal government expenditure stands at around Rs19 trillion, while total tax and non-tax revenue was Rs20tr, leaving nothing for the provinces and forcing the federal government to resort to heavy borrowing,” Ghumro said.

The PPP senator contended that had the government implemented the 18th Amendment , devolved provincial matters and handed over CCI matters to the permanent secretariat of the CCI as envisaged under Article 154 of the Constitution, the country would not have needed handouts from the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
During the last 15 years, the IMF gave Pakistan $15bn, while the government spent $18bn to $20bn on devolved ministries and institutions, he claimed.
“Had this amount been spent on infrastructure and social development, Pakistan would have been a different country.
“A taxpayer’s hard-earned money had been consigned to unauthorised expenditure,” he added.

The convener said the federal government makes two kinds of expenditure from the Federal Consolidated Fund: “charged expenditure” on remuneration and other perks of the president, Senate chair and deputy chair, National Assembly speaker and deputy speaker, auditor general, high court and Supreme Court judges; and debt servicing, which the NA does not vote on, and “other expenditure” in the form of demands for grants by federal ministries created on federal subjects.
“It must not spend a penny on provincial or other purposes,” Senator Ghumro stressed.
“This is taxpayers’ money paid to the federal government to be spent for the purposes and services rendered by the federal government under the Constitution.
“The federal government is not obliged to provide health, education, housing, sanitation, water or other services for which the Constitution empowers provincial governments.”

Senator Ghumro added: “A citizen cannot pay the federal government for purposes and services not rendered by it under the Constitution; hence such unauthorised expenditure of more than Rs5tr amounts to gross misuse of authority under the law and Constitution and must be accounted for legally.”
He said neither the Ministry of Finance can send demands for grants for such expenditure nor the auditor general or Accountant General of Pakistan can authorise it.
They have to see that the expenditure is for purposes and services to be provided by the federal government under the Constitution, he said.
“Those matters are specifically mentioned in the Federal Legislative List . All powers under Article 142 are vested in the provinces except those enumerated for the federation in the Federal List.”

Senator Ghumro said that, under Article 154 (functions and rules of procedure of CCI) read with Article 97 (extent of executive authority of federation), executive authority over subjects mentioned in the Federal Legislative List’s Part II is to be exercised by the CCI and not the federal cabinet.

The convener noted that the CCI and Cabinet Division had sent summaries to the prime minister to abolish 24 ministries and institutions, thus curtailing federal expenditure, but the prime minister had yet to respond.
He said that, even otherwise, such ministries would become redundant as the Auditor General of Pakistan and the finance ministry would not allow such expenditure.
He directed the CCI and Cabinet Division to send a fresh note to the prime minister for abolition of ministries on provincial and CCI matters.
In July, the Functional Committee on Devolution had expressed serious concerns over the re-establishment of federal ministries on subjects devolved to the provinces under the 18th Amendment.
It had also constituted a sub-committee to examine the alleged violations.
During a meeting of that sub-committee last month, senators sought a probe into a staggering Rs2.6 trillion expenditure by the federal government on education and health ministries.
Provinces’ share in federal appointments
The sub-committee also took up the matter of shares of provinces in federal appointments in ministries and corporations.

The Establishment Division informed the committee that, as per its instructions, 5,000 jobs of Balochistan had been advertised to rectify its share as required under Article 38(g) of the Constitution.

Senator Ghumro said the committee had identified a shortage of more than 30,000 jobs in Balochistan’s share, which must be filled. The convener noted that a shortage of more than 80,000 jobs had been pointed out in Sindh, and that positions must be advertised to rectify it.

The Federal Public Service Commission secretary informed the sub-committee that appointments for the shares of Sindh and Balochistan in services would be expedited as they had cleared the earlier backlog. He said a special CSS examination was conducted for these provinces.
The sub-committee observed that there was a meagre number of appointments of secretaries, CEOs and other high positions from Sindh and Balochistan.
The convener said Article 38(g) envisages shares in all grades, and the federal government must submit a grade-wise position in grades 18 to 22 in 15 days.

It must expedite the process through ministries in grades 1-15 positions, by FPSC in grades 16 and 17 positions and in grades 18 to 22 by the federal government and the prime minister. Compliance must be substantive and practical, he said.
The Senate panel called for implementation, rather than “statements of intent”.

It also expressed displeasure over the non-submission of a report by the information ministry, which had sought a month to devolve print media organisations and functions at the federal level and develop a mechanism to give broadcasting rights to provinces under Article 159 of the Constitution.
It directed the ministry to finalise all issues in 15 days and submit compliance.
‘Highly sophisticated silver swapping case’

Meanwhile, a separate Senate panel was briefed by the Federal Investigation Agency’s (FIA) Anti-Corruption Circle on a coordinated multi-city operation in connection with the silver swapping and heist case earlier this year — involving alleged corruption, smuggling and suspected involvement of officials.
Senator Saifullah Abro chaired a meeting of a sub-committee of the Senate Standing Committee on Interior and Narcotics Control.

The panel was informed that during the investigation, it was revealed that the suspects had allegedly adopted a systematic modus operandi involving fabrication of fake container seals, counterfeiting, substitution of genuine silver with lead bars and concealment of the stolen consignment.

The investigation established that approximately 400 kilogrammes of silver had been swapped, out of which 214kg had so far been recovered, while the case involved an estimated financial loss of Rs4m. Legal proceedings had been initiated against the suspects, who were facing proceedings before competent courts.
The FIA said the investigation was continuing through digital and financial forensics, asset tracing and other measures to identify all individuals involved and recover the remaining stolen silver.
The Safe City director general explained that the theft had been carried out in a highly sophisticated and carefully planned manner.

When the consignment reached Lahore, it was discovered that the original silver had been replaced with lead bars. He explained that one vehicle had initially been prepared for the operation. However, as it exited the airport, another identical vehicle approached from behind and carried out the swapping operation. The vehicle carrying the consignment was subsequently taken away. The entire sequence was detected through the Safe City surveillance system.

Further investigation revealed that replica boxes had been prepared specifically for the operation, and the individual suspected of manufacturing and supplying these boxes was apprehended after four weeks.
The Safe City DG also questioned the allegations of their involvement, stating that had they been involved, they would not have detected and exposed the swapping activity themselves.
The chairman appreciated the FIA’s efforts and lauded the recovery of 214kg of silver.
Abro remarked that the incident deserved to be made into a film.

He suggested that if Sindh had a dedicated film-making wing, or a similar facility existed in Balochistan, a film should be produced highlighting the entire incident, particularly how the theft was planned and executed and how it was subsequently detected through the Safe City surveillance system.
The meeting was attended by Senator Umer Farooq and senior officials from relevant ministries and departments.
Records sought from FBR

The panel led by Abro also ordered the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) to bring complete records of consumption certificates, payments and verification documents to an in-camera meeting on Nov 16, as it pursued the alleged misuse of the Fata/Pata tax exemption scheme involving imports worth Rs1,120bn and recovery of evaded taxes.

The chairman expressed serious displeasure over the absence of the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency’s (NCCIA) DG, questioning the “non-serious” attitude of the authorities, particularly when it had already been decided in the previous meeting that the DG would brief the committee.

During the briefing, representatives of FBR and FIA presented their respective positions. The FBR maintained that it had not received any formal notice from the court, whereas the FIA informed the committee that its legal adviser had received the relevant court order.
Senator Abro and panel members expressed concern over the apparent lack of coordination and questioned why the FBR had remained unaware of the court proceedings for nearly two months.

The committee was briefed on the reconciliation gap between Customs import data and consumption certificates for the period from 2018 to June 2026. It was informed that total imports amounted to Rs1,120.66 billion, against which consumption certificates covered imports worth Rs389.87bn, leaving an apparent unreconciled difference of Rs730.80bn.

The sector-wise analysis revealed apparent differences of Rs148.25bn in steel, Rs146.96bn in textile/fabric, Rs100.88bnin food, and Rs76.49bn in ghee and oil. The committee emphasised the need for a comprehensive, transaction-wise reconciliation to ascertain the actual position and determine any potential tax liability or revenue loss.

The FIA informed the committee that 512 notices had been issued to various companies in connection with the ongoing investigation, out of which 19 companies joined the proceedings with partial records, while more than 100 notices were returned or remained undelivered. The matter is under examination before the competent court, and proceedings are investigative in nature, aimed at obtaining relevant documents and explanations.
Possible corruption, abuse of authority, diversion and wrongful release of securities are being independently examined in accordance with the law, the FIA added.
Senator Abro said the committee had been pursuing the matter for a considerable period and the authorities must demonstrate seriousness and take concrete action instead of prolonging the proceedings.

The panel was also briefed about the FBR’s reluctance to share relevant records with the parliamentary committee, particularly when the department was prepared to provide information to the court and other authorities.

Referring to Article 66 of the Constitution, Senator Abro asked the FBR to clarify the authorities to whom such records could legally be disclosed. The members stressed that parliamentary oversight must be respected and that legal provisions should not be used to delay accountability.

The chairman sought a comprehensive explanation of the certificates, the amounts released against them and the supporting documentation. He particularly highlighted 20 certificates involving approximately Rs64bn and directed the FBR to provide complete details, including records and justification for their issuance. He further referred to the terms of reference concerning approximately Rs74bn and questioned the release of payments without adequate verification and scrutiny.

Expressing serious concern over the financial implications, the chairman observed that the alleged tax liability associated with the matter could be substantial and that the state must recover every rupee legally due. He referred to an estimated amount of Rs1,120bn and stressed that the FBR must ensure proper assessment and recovery of applicable taxes.

Senator Abro directed the FBR to examine the relevant Statement of Requirements (SOR) issued in 2021 and investigate whether the consumption certificates and subsequent releases had been processed in accordance with the applicable legal framework.

The chairman also raised concerns regarding the large number of companies and petitioners involved in the proceedings and directed the FBR to examine the list of petitioners, verify their respective positions and issue notices wherever necessary.

Referring to reports of individuals possessing substantial assets, large convoys of vehicles and unexplained sources of income, Senator Abro urged the FBR to investigate possible financial irregularities and money laundering. The members stressed that the investigation must also examine financial trails and possible involvement of influential individuals and networks.

The committee further discussed the alleged movement and importation of tobacco-related material through the Fata/Pata exemption regime and its subsequent use by companies operating outside the exempted areas.
The chairman observed that the issue involved a substantial loss to the national exchequer and required coordinated action by the FIA, FBR, Customs and other enforcement agencies.
He directed the authorities to provide complete import records from January 2018 onwards, particularly details of consignments, their movement, destinations and companies involved.

He also sought details of companies involved in importing material without payment of applicable taxes and directed Customs authorities to furnish records of imports through Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and former Fata areas, particularly for the period after June 2026. He emphasised the need to examine the tracking and movement of containers and to identify any misuse of the exemption mechanism through companies established in other parts of the country. The committee was informed that a significant number of companies had already been referred to the FIA for investigation, while further cases remained under examination.

The chairman stressed that the investigation must be pursued without “fear or favour”, observing that the money involved belonged to the people of Pakistan. He also emphasised that wherever law-and-order constraints prevented officials from accessing certain factories, assistance of law enforcement agencies should be sought.
The chairman directed that the next meeting, scheduled for Nov 16, be held in camera to examine sensitive financial and investigative records.

The FBR was directed to bring complete details of all consumption certificates issued from Nov 2025 onwards, along with corresponding payments, pay orders, supporting documents and verification records. The authorities were also directed to provide complete details of the remaining companies under investigation without further delay.

Furthermore, the KP Customs authorities were given four to five working days to furnish the required import and movement records, taking into account different routes and customs regimes through which consignments had been processed. The chairman directed that all relevant information be compiled and presented before the committee in the next in-camera meeting.

cards.title: PM Shehbaz stresses clean energy’s importance for Pakistan at Chashma-5 nuclear plant event
cards.author: News Desk
cards.why: It covers Pakistan's energy mix, nuclear power and Pakistan-China cooperation.
cards.summary: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif spoke at the dome placement ceremony of the Chashma-5 nuclear power plant near Mianwali. Dome placement marks the end of civil works and the start of internal installation. The 1,200MW plant, built with Chinese help, is expected to begin generating power in September 2030. The PM praised nuclear energy as clean and reliable and thanked China for its support.
key_facts: Chashma-5 (C-5) near Mianwali will have a capacity of 1,200MW.
C-5 is expected to start generating electricity in September 2030.
C-5 is Pakistan's seventh nuclear plant built with China's help; its groundbreaking was in July 2023.
Pakistan's nuclear plants generate 3,530MW and avoid 15 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions a year.
Nuclear energy provides about 16.6pc of Pakistan's electricity generation from 8.6pc of installed capacity, rising to 26pc in winter.
Dr Raja Ali Raza Anwar is chairman of the Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission.

vocab.meaning: an important stage in progress

cards.title: PM Shehbaz arrives in Turkiye to address COP31 summit
cards.author: News Desk, AFP
cards.why: COP31, climate finance and Pakistan's climate diplomacy are key Current Affairs topics.
cards.summary: PM Shehbaz Sharif arrived in Antalya, Turkiye, for the COP31 Leaders' Summit of the UNFCCC. He plans to highlight Pakistan's solarisation, early-warning efforts and the need for accessible climate finance. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged a faster move away from fossil fuels, while Turkish President Erdogan welcomed the discovery of new oil fields. The talks began with a dispute over putting climate finance on the agenda.
key_facts: COP31, the 31st Conference of the Parties to the UNFCCC, is being held in Antalya, Turkiye, in November 2026.
The COP31 presidency held a high-level dialogue on clean energy titled '35 by 35: Powering the Future'.
A Pakistan Pavilion at COP31 will host 54 events.
President Erdogan announced two oil fields potentially holding 135 million barrels of crude.
At COP30 in Brazil, fossil fuels were not named in the final agreement.
The EU's climate monitor said 2026 would most likely be the second-hottest year on record.

vocab.meaning: changing energy use to run on electricity

cards.title: Trump nominates Natalie Baker for US ambassador to Pakistan
cards.author: News Desk
cards.why: It is an appointment relevant to Pakistan-US relations.
cards.summary: President Donald Trump has nominated Natalie Baker as US ambassador to Pakistan. She has been chargé d'affaires in Islamabad since January 2025, after ambassador Donald Armin Blome left. The nomination now goes to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and then the full Senate. Baker earlier served in Doha, Libya, Dubai and Kuwait.
key_facts: Natalie Baker was nominated by President Trump as US ambassador to Pakistan in November 2026.
Baker became chargé d'affaires at the US embassy in Islamabad in January 2025.
She replaced the departed ambassador Donald Armin Blome as head of the mission.
She served as deputy chief of mission in Doha from August 2021 to July 2024.

vocab.meaning: a diplomat who leads an embassy when there is no ambassador

cards.title: Lahore’s PM2.5 level eight times WHO guideline, report says
cards.author: Imran Gabol
cards.why: Smog and air pollution are major Environment and governance issues in Punjab.
cards.summary: A Pakistan Air Quality Initiative report found 16,714 likely crop-residue fires in Punjab between October 1 and November 9, while Lahore's average PM2.5 was eight times the WHO guideline. Pollution in Lahore was higher on days when winds passed over burning areas. The report said evidence did not support blaming Lahore's post-Diwali smog on Indian fireworks. Punjab's environment department reported improvement after anti-smog operations, and rain is forecast.
key_facts: Lahore's average PM2.5 was 126 micrograms per cubic metre from October 1 to November 9, 2026, eight times the WHO guideline.
Satellites detected 18,825 fires across Pakistani Punjab, 89pc of them likely crop-residue burning.
Sheikhupura recorded the most fires (2,559), followed by Jhang, Okara, Hafizabad and Gujranwala.
Lahore's PM2.5 averaged 175 micrograms on days with air from burning areas, compared with 93 on other days.
Lahore's average AQI fell from 489 to 232 on one day after anti-smog operations, a drop of about 53pc.

vocab.meaning: very small particles in the air that can enter the lungs
the path that air or an object follows

cards.title: US calls for new Europe security framework as Russia, Ukraine hold first peace talks in 9 months
cards.author: AFP
cards.why: The Russia-Ukraine peace process shapes global security and International Relations.
cards.summary: US-led talks between Russia and Ukraine began in Abu Dhabi, the first since February. Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff said the US wants a new security framework for Ukraine, Russia and Europe. Europe fears a US-Russia deal over its future, and Ukraine warned against a 'Yalta 2.0'. Ukraine seeks a ceasefire, security guarantees and long-term support for its army.
key_facts: In November 2026, Russia and Ukraine held US-led talks in Abu Dhabi, the first in nine months.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff led the talks.
Rustem Umerov is Ukraine's chief negotiator.
A local truce in Ukraine's Kherson region, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, was the longest pause in the war.
Ukraine wants at least 10 years of financial support for an 800,000-strong army.

vocab.meaning: a basic structure for an agreement
existing in reality, even if not officially

cards.title: Vanishing vessels and missing sailors: The Iran war's human cost at sea
cards.author: Reuters
cards.why: It shows the impact of the Iran war on Gulf shipping and the Strait of Hormuz.
cards.summary: A Reuters report describes the human cost of attacks on shipping since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28. Two Bolivian-flagged vessels, Bridge 1 and Bridge 2, vanished near Iran's Kish Island in May with six crew, including one Pakistani. The IMO has confirmed 130 incidents in the region, with at least 25 seafarers killed. Crew hiring costs have tripled as risks grow.
key_facts: The US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28, 2026.
The International Maritime Organisation confirmed 130 incidents, mainly attacks, in the region, with at least 25 seafarers killed.
The vessels Bridge 1 and Bridge 2 disappeared about 8 nautical miles from Iran's Kish Island on May 9.
The missing crew included three Iraqis, two Indians and one Pakistani.
India's Seamen's Employment Office withdrew the licence of Lascar Marine Services for failing to repatriate seafarers.

vocab.meaning: to send someone back to their own country
shock and worry

mcqs.q: According to the World Bank's Pakistan Poverty and Equity brief released in 2026, what was Pakistan's national poverty rate in 2024-25?
mcqs.explanation: The rate rose from 22pc in 2018-19 to 29pc in 2024-25, about 70 million people. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: The UNDP's 2025 Global Multidimensional Poverty Index found what share of Pakistan's population to be multidimensionally poor?
mcqs.explanation: It found 38.3pc of Pakistanis, about 95 million people, multidimensionally poor, against 16.4pc in India and 14.9pc in Bangladesh. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: What was Pakistan's rank in the 2026 Global Hunger Index?
mcqs.explanation: Pakistan ranked 106th of 122 countries and had the highest hunger score in South Asia. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: In the UNDP Human Development Report 2025, Pakistan was ranked:
mcqs.explanation: Pakistan was placed 168th of 193 countries in the 'low' human development category. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: Pakistan's Gini index rose to which level, the highest in 25 years, according to the World Bank's 2026 poverty brief?
mcqs.explanation: The Gini index, a measure of inequality, rose from 28.4 to 32.7. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: Pakistan is ranked 89th among 145 countries in which index produced by Harvard?
mcqs.explanation: Harvard's Economic Complexity Index ranks Pakistan 89th of 145, reflecting the low quality of its exports. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: In which city was the COP31 UN climate conference held in November 2026?
mcqs.explanation: COP31 of the UNFCCC was held in Antalya, Turkiye; PM Shehbaz Sharif attended its Leaders' Summit. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: What is the planned generation capacity of the Chashma-5 nuclear power plant near Mianwali?
mcqs.explanation: C-5 will generate 1,200MW and is expected to begin generation in September 2030. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: When is the Chashma-5 nuclear power plant expected to begin generating electricity?
mcqs.explanation: The government said C-5 is expected to start generation in September 2030; its dome was placed in November 2026. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: In late 2026, nuclear energy accounted for about what share of Pakistan's electricity generation?
mcqs.explanation: Nuclear provided about 16.6pc of generation from only 8.6pc of installed capacity, rising to 26pc in winter. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: Chashma-5 is Pakistan's which nuclear power plant built with the help of China?
mcqs.explanation: PM Shehbaz described C-5 as Pakistan's seventh nuclear plant built with Chinese assistance. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: In November 2026, US President Donald Trump nominated whom as US ambassador to Pakistan?
mcqs.explanation: Natalie Baker, chargé d'affaires in Islamabad since January 2025, was nominated; the Senate must confirm her. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: A Pakistan Air Quality Initiative report found Lahore's average PM2.5 from October 1 to November 9, 2026 to be how many times the WHO guideline?
mcqs.explanation: Lahore averaged 126 micrograms per cubic metre, eight times the WHO guideline value. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: Which Punjab district recorded the highest number of satellite-detected fires between October 1 and November 9, 2026?
mcqs.explanation: Sheikhupura had 2,559 fires, followed by Jhang, Okara, Hafizabad and Gujranwala. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: In November 2026, where were US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine held, the first in nine months?
mcqs.explanation: Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff hosted the talks in Abu Dhabi. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: A local truce in Ukraine's Kherson region, the longest pause in the war by late 2026, was brokered by:
mcqs.explanation: US First Lady Melania Trump brokered the Kherson truce in October 2026. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: How many incidents in the Gulf region had the International Maritime Organisation confirmed since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28, 2026?
mcqs.explanation: The IMO confirmed 130 incidents, mainly attacks, with at least 25 seafarers killed. (The Express Tribune)

mcqs.q: By late 2026, how much money was available in the Loss and Damage Fund against $2.8 billion in requests?
mcqs.explanation: The fund had $342 million; Pakistan's $58 million in proposals got no allocation. (The Express Tribune)

mcqs.q: Pakistan estimates it will need how much money by 2035 to meet its climate commitments?
mcqs.explanation: Islamabad estimates $565 billion by 2035, while over 60pc of revenue goes to debt servicing. (The Express Tribune)

mcqs.q: Which Article of the Constitution of Pakistan deals with the functions and rules of procedure of the Council of Common Interests?
mcqs.explanation: A Senate panel head cited Article 154 while saying CCI matters should go to the CCI secretariat. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: Which Article of the Constitution of Pakistan was cited by a Senate panel in 2026 for provincial shares in federal service jobs?
mcqs.explanation: The panel cited Article 38(g) and found shortages of over 30,000 jobs for Balochistan and 80,000 for Sindh. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: In 2026, a Senate panel head said the federal government had spent more than how much on devolved provincial subjects and CCI matters?
mcqs.explanation: Senator Zamir Hussain Ghumro cited the Auditor General's report for spending of over Rs5 trillion (over $18 billion). (Dawn)

mcqs.q: The 2026 UN assessment 'Extreme Heat and Agriculture' was prepared by the FAO and which other body?
mcqs.explanation: The FAO and WMO assessment found that heat is cutting farm output; fruit yields in Punjab's high-rainfall areas have halved. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: After Israel's October 2026 election, the Israeli president asked whom to form a government?
mcqs.explanation: Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot was asked to form a government, while Netanyahu remained caretaker prime minister. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: In the US midterm elections of November 2026, who became the first Native American woman elected to the US Senate?
mcqs.explanation: Peggy Flanagan won in Minnesota as Democrats took control of both houses of Congress. (Dawn)

mcqs.q: Pakistan's 2022 floods affected about how many people?
mcqs.explanation: The floods submerged a third of the country, affected 33 million people and caused over $30 billion in damage. (The Express Tribune)
